primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's November 27, 1992 speech before the National Convention of Dominican and Siena Schools at Siena College, Quezon City, explaining 'Lay Empowerment in Building a Community of Believers' as decreed by PCP II and Vatican II, delivered as one of the lay delegates who took part in PCP II's lawmaking.

The two fundamental aspects of the lay vocation under PCP II (405): that the lay faithful belong fully to the Church as co-workers 'equal in dignity and in mission to the clergy,' and that their vocation remains secular -- lived out in politics, government, business, industry and finance rather than withdrawn from them.

The source and meaning of lay 'empowerment' -- baptism and confirmation incorporating the laity into Christ so that they 'share in the priestly, prophetic and kingly office of Christ' -- and the four essentials for exercising it effectively: genuine conversion of mind and heart, renewed catechesis, renewed worship and renewed social apostolate.

The four areas where the laity is called to use that empowerment -- a community of families, Christian presence in the world, service and evangelization, and social transformation -- closing with the statistic that 88 percent of Filipino Catholics are 'unchurched, uninvolved and untouched by the parish' and are the great challenge before Catholic educators.
sub_topics: Opening self-deprecation: CJP admits he 'seldom accept[s] speaking engagement before educators, nuns and priests' because a survey placed priests and nuns first in credibility and teachers second, while politicians came last and lawyers second to the last.

The balloon joke and the epitaph: two lost lady balloonists identify the man below as a lawyer because his answer was 'very accurate but entirely useless,' and an English epitaph reads 'Here lies lawyer John Quill; he lies still' -- a lament about 'lawyers being useless hair-splitters and consummate talkers.'
Teachers' nobility: their 'influence is eternal,' passed from pupils to their children's children, which is why Jesus chose to be a teacher and was called 'Rabbi.'

Who the laity are: per Lumen Gentium, all the baptized except those in Holy Orders or an approved religious state -- and since Vatican II and PCP II call the Church the 'People of God,' the laity are 'the overwhelming 99 percent of its membership.'

First aspect -- full belonging: the lay faithful 'are not second-class members,' not 'deputies or assistants or helpers of priests' but co-workers; the hierarchy remains but is 'a hierarchy of service and not of excellence,' since 'the Christian dignity of the ordained is measured by the sincerity and genuineness of their service rather than by the office they hold' (PCP II, 96).

A consequence of that equality: lay organizations no longer need a mandate from the hierarchy, so bodies like the Council of the Laity, the Catholic Women's League and the Apostleship of Prayer are now called 'traditional' rather than 'mandated' organizations.

Second aspect -- the secular character: the laity are 'to seek the Kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs,' so lawyers must stay lawyers, 'Christians cannot shun politics because it is dirty,' and teachers must find holiness in teaching -- with James 3 warning that teachers 'will be called to stricter account.'

His daughter Mabel's vocation: told she felt called to be an Opus Dei numerary, he asked 'bakit hindi ka na lang maging madre?' and only later understood that numeraries 'do not lose their lay character' and must work 'amidst the noise and banging of the world.'

Where empowerment comes from: by baptism and confirmation the laity are incorporated into Christ and 'share in the priestly, prophetic and kingly office of Christ,' becoming 'a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation' -- an apostolate 'of divine right' (PCP II, 408) -- so their status is not elevated, only their duty to evangelize emphasized.

First essential -- genuine conversion: a 'change of heart, metanoia,' usually 'a day-to-day grinding, grasping and following of Christ,' though instant conversions occur, as with Peter, Andrew, James and John, St. Paul on the road to Damascus, and the repentant thief; illustrated by Johnny, who could not date Christ's birth but had stopped drinking, gambling and womanizing.

Second essential -- renewed catechesis (not catechism), which must be Christo-centric, rooted in the Word of God, authentically Filipino (answering 'the death penalty, the right to life of the unborn and the untangling of the debt burden') and systematic, as teachers' own syllabi are.

Third essential -- renewed worship, which is 'personal... familial... communal': he once thought God 'was someone apart' too great for small problems, but now knows 'our God is a personal God, a caring God,' and prayer means 'Thy will be done,' not dictating our own designs.

Fourth essential -- renewed social apostolate: 'We cannot go to heaven alone,' for at the final judgment God will ask not about bank digits, Mercedeses or PhDs but 'what we did for the least of our brethren' (Matt. 25:31-46); and PCP II warns that the four elements are interdependent -- catechesis without social apostolate 'will not transform,' worship without catechesis 'degenerate[s] into formalism.'

The four areas of the laity's role: a Community of Families ('The family is the Church in the home'); Christian presence in the world; service and evangelization -- where mere 'bait-Pinoy' obedience to the negative commandments is not enough, since Msgr. Bayani Valenzuela says St. Peter 'hahanapin din po niya ang ating buting-Pinoy'; and social transformation, in which Christian presence 'permeates every beat of life,' as with PPCRV's work in the last elections.

The closing statistics: parish priests minister to 40,000-50,000 parishioners; CBCP studies show only two percent of Catholics are active and 10 percent are regular churchgoers, with the sacraments taken mostly by the 'highly audible-visible' women and the men largely 'reluctant' -- leaving 88 percent 'unchurched, uninvolved and untouched by the parish' as the great challenge to educators, 'the successors in the profession of Christ.'

stances.claim: The lay faithful are not second-class members of the Church but co-workers 'equal in dignity and in mission to the clergy,' since the hierarchy that remains is 'a hierarchy of service and not of excellence.'
stances.rhetorical_move: conciliar-citation: grounding lay equality in PCP II 405 and 96 and Lumen Gentium rather than in argument of his own

stances.claim: The laity must not retreat from the secular world because it is sinful -- lawyers must stay lawyers, 'Christians cannot shun politics because it is dirty,' and teachers must find holiness in teaching.
stances.rhetorical_move: vocation-in-place: turning the secular character of the lay vocation into a duty to stay and clean up one's own milieu

stances.claim: Possessing lay empowerment is worthless unless exercised, and its effective exercise requires all four of genuine conversion, renewed catechesis, renewed worship and renewed social apostolate together.
stances.rhetorical_move: fourfold-test with interlocking warnings -- catechesis without social apostolate 'will not transform,' worship without catechesis becomes 'formalism,' apostolate alone is 'mere activism'

stances.claim: It is not enough to keep the negative commandments -- 'bait-Pinoy' obedience must become 'buting-Pinoy,' actively doing good for one's neighbor.
stances.rhetorical_move: vernacular-coinage: a Tagalog wordplay, backed by Msgr. Valenzuela's line about St. Peter, to make Matthew 25 memorable

stances.claim: The 88 percent of Catholics who are 'unchurched, uninvolved and untouched by the parish' are the great challenge, and empowered lay educators are called to re-evangelize them.
stances.rhetorical_move: statistics-to-summons: closing with CBCP figures and turning them into a direct challenge to his audience

notable_anecdotes: The lost balloonists: two ladies drifting over European borders are told exactly where they are -- 'in a wooden cart attached to a balloon' -- and conclude the man must be a lawyer, since his answer was 'very accurate but entirely useless.'
The epitaph: he quotes an English cemetery marker, 'Here lies lawyer John Quill; he lies still,' as the centuries-old lament about lawyers.

Mabel and Opus Dei: his daughter told him she was called to be a numerary, and he replied 'Hija, bakit hindi ka na lang maging madre?' before understanding that she was 'called to remain lay, not to be a religious.'

Johnny the instant convert: quizzed on the year of Christ's birth, His nationality and His age at death, Johnny knew none of it but answered that since meeting the Lord he had stopped drinking and gambling and there was 'only one woman in my life - my beautiful wife.'

Learning that God is personal: CJP recalls believing God 'was someone apart - so powerful and so great that I could not bother Him with my little problems,' and now consulting Him even on where to park or which road to take.
PCP II as lay empowerment in the flesh: he notes that for the first time in nearly 2,000 years lay men and women debated and voted -- if only 'consultative[ly]' -- in the Church's lawmaking.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Love God, Serve Man' records CJP's November 27, 1992 speech at Siena College, Quezon City, before the National Convention of Dominican and Siena Schools, on 'Lay Empowerment in Building a Community of Believers' as decreed by PCP II and Vatican II. He opened by confessing that he rarely addressed educators, nuns and priests, since a survey ranked them highest in credibility while lawyers stood second to last -- a point he illustrated with the joke of the lost balloonists told their exact position 'accurate but entirely useless,' and the epitaph 'Here lies lawyer John Quill; he lies still.' Defining the laity from Lumen Gentium as all the baptized outside Holy Orders and the religious state, he noted that in a Church now called the 'People of God' they form 99 percent of the membership. He then set out PCP II's two fundamental aspects of the lay vocation: full belonging, so that lay people are 'not second-class members' but co-workers equal in dignity and mission, the remaining hierarchy being 'a hierarchy of service and not of excellence'; and secular character, so that lawyers stay lawyers, teachers find holiness in teaching, and 'Christians cannot shun politics because it is dirty' -- a point he illustrated with his daughter Mabel's call to be an Opus Dei numerary, which he first misunderstood. Empowerment, he explained, comes directly from Christ through baptism and confirmation, giving the laity a share in His 'priestly, prophetic and kingly office'; but possessing it is not using it, and its effective exercise requires four things together -- genuine conversion of mind and heart, renewed catechesis (Christo-centric, biblical, authentically Filipino, systematic), renewed worship, and renewed social apostolate -- since each is deficient without the others. He listed the four areas of the lay calling, insisted that 'bait-Pinoy' must become 'buting-Pinoy,' and closed with CBCP figures showing 88 percent of Catholics 'unchurched, uninvolved and untouched by the parish,' challenging the teachers before him, 'the successors in the profession of Christ,' to answer God's challenge.
